title: Linked list: reverse a sublist
summary: Reverse positions left..right (1-based) of a linked list in one pass. A dummy head covers left = 1; flip next pointers inside the range, then reconnect both ends. O(n), O(1) space. The Node class is shown, not typed.
code:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, value, next_node=None):
        self.value = value
        self.next = next_node

# Flip next pointers inside the range, then reconnect both ends.
def reverse_between(head, left, right):
    dummy = Node(0, head)
    before = dummy
    for _ in range(left - 1):
        before = before.next
    previous, current = None, before.next
    for _ in range(right - left + 1):
        following = current.next
        current.next = previous
        previous, current = current, following
    before.next.next = current
    before.next = previous
    return dummy.next

prompts: A playlist is stored as a chain of tracks, each pointing to the next. Reverse the order of tracks 3 through 7 in place.

pitfalls: Save current.next before overwriting it, or the rest of the list is lost.

title: Monotonic stack: largest rectangle
summary: Largest rectangle under a histogram. Keep bar indices with rising heights; a shorter bar pops each taller one and measures how far it spans. A trailing 0 flushes the stack. O(n).
code:
# Heights rise up the stack; a shorter bar closes every taller one.
def largest_rectangle(heights):
    stack = []
    best = 0
    for index, height in enumerate(heights + [0]):
        while stack and heights[stack[-1]] >= height:
            top = heights[stack.pop()]
            width = index if not stack else index - stack[-1] - 1
            best = max(best, top * width)
        stack.append(index)
    return best

title: Topological sort: Kahn's algorithm
summary: An order of courses 0..n-1 that respects every (before, after) prerequisite, or [] if there is a cycle. Start with the courses that have none; finishing one lowers each dependent's in-degree, and a dependent at 0 is ready. O(V + E).
code:
from collections import deque

# Take any course with no unmet prerequisites; leftovers sit on a cycle.
def course_order(n, prerequisites):
    graph = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    indegree = [0] * n
    for before, after in prerequisites:
        graph[before].append(after)
        indegree[after] += 1
    queue = deque(node for node in range(n) if indegree[node] == 0)
    order = []
    while queue:
        before = queue.popleft()
        order.append(before)
        for after in graph[before]:
            indegree[after] -= 1
            if indegree[after] == 0:
                queue.append(after)
    return order if len(order) == n else []
triggers: order tasks so every dependency comes first
decide whether dependencies contain a cycle
prompts: A build system knows which modules need which others compiled first. Produce a compile order, or report that none exists.
A recipe lists steps and which steps must finish before others can start. Find an order to do them all, or show that the recipe is impossible.
invariant: Every course in the queue or in order has all of its prerequisites earlier in order.
mantra: Start with no prerequisites; a course is ready when its in-degree hits 0.
pitfalls: Count every in-degree before seeding the queue.
Fewer than n courses in order means the rest sit on a cycle: return [].
Edges point from prerequisite to dependent; reversing them reverses the order.
Many valid orders can exist; check the edges rather than one expected list.

anchors.name: Course Schedule
anchors.trick: Only ask whether len(order) == n.

anchors.name: Course Schedule II
anchors.trick: Exactly this.

anchors.name: Alien Dictionary
anchors.trick: The first differing letters of adjacent words give the edges; then sort.

anchors.name: Parallel Courses
anchors.trick: Process the queue level by level; the number of levels is the number of semesters.

mutations.explanation: On a cycle it returns a partial order instead of [], hiding the courses that can never be taken.
Decrements the finished course instead of its dependent, so dependents never reach 0 and valid schedules come back empty.

title: Graph DFS: iterative reachability
summary: Every node reachable from start, using an explicit stack instead of recursion. A node is marked when popped, so it may be pushed twice; BFS marks on enqueue instead. O(V + E).
triggers: reachability or connected components: can A reach B, how many groups
follow one branch to the end before backing up: cycles, ordering, flood fill
prompts: Installing one package pulls in its dependencies, and theirs in turn. List every package that installing a given one brings along.
Rooms are linked by one-way doors. Starting in the lobby, which rooms can a visitor ever reach?
invariant: visited holds exactly the expanded nodes, and every node on the stack is reachable from start.
mantra: Pop, skip if seen, mark, push the unseen neighbours.
pitfalls: Marking on pop allows duplicates on the stack, so the 'if node in visited: continue' guard is required.
Recursive DFS is shorter, but Python's default recursion limit is about 1000 frames.
Cycle detection in a directed graph needs three states: unvisited, on the current path, done.

anchors.name: Number of Islands
anchors.trick: Start a DFS from each unvisited land cell; count the starts.

anchors.name: Clone Graph
anchors.trick: The original-to-copy map doubles as the visited set.

anchors.name: Course Schedule
anchors.trick: Three-state DFS: reaching an on-path node means a cycle.

anchors.name: Keys and Rooms
anchors.trick: Exactly this: is every room reachable from room 0?

mutations.explanation: Peeks instead of popping: once the top node is visited, the loop spins on it forever.

title: Tree DFS: return values up
summary: Diameter of a binary tree: the most edges on any path between two nodes. A post-order helper returns each subtree's height and records the best path through the current node on the way up. O(n). The TreeNode class is shown, not typed.
triggers: an answer for the whole tree built from answers for its subtrees
a path that may bend at any node: combine the left and right results there
prompts: Reporting lines form a tree in which each manager has at most two direct reports. How many reporting links separate the two people who are farthest apart?
A cave system branches like a binary tree from its entrance, and passages never rejoin. Counting passages, how long is the longest route between any two chambers?
invariant: height(node) returns the number of nodes on the longest downward path from node, and best is the longest path, in edges, through any node finished so far.
mantra: Return the height up; record left + right on the way.
pitfalls: What a call returns (height) differs from what it records (diameter): keep both straight.
Diameter counts edges: left + right, not left + right + 1.
Use nonlocal, or a one-element list, to update best from the nested function.
A deep, one-sided tree can hit Python's recursion limit of about 1000.

anchors.name: Diameter of Binary Tree
anchors.trick: Exactly this.

anchors.name: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
anchors.trick: Only the returned height: 1 + max(left, right).

anchors.name: Balanced Binary Tree
anchors.trick: Return the height, or -1 once the two sides differ by more than 1.

anchors.name: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
anchors.trick: Return value + the better non-negative side; record value + both non-negative sides.

mutations.explanation: Never counts the current node, so every height is 0 and the diameter is always 0.
Counts nodes instead of edges: a single node reports 1 instead of 0.

title: Backtracking: subsets
summary: Every subset of distinct values. Record a copy of path, then for each later index choose it, recurse from index + 1, and undo. O(n * 2^n).
code:
# Each recursive call extends a choice made so far.
def subsets(values):
    result = []
    path = []
    def visit(start):
        result.append(path.copy())
        for index in range(start, len(values)):
            path.append(values[index])
            visit(index + 1)
            path.pop()
    visit(0)
    return result
triggers: list every subset, combination, permutation or arrangement
choices with undo, and n small enough (about 20) for exponential output
prompts: A pizza shop offers a handful of toppings. List every possible topping selection, including a plain pizza.
A tester wants to try every combination of a few feature flags being switched on. Generate them all.
invariant: On entry to visit(start), path is a subset of values[:start] in index order, and only values[start:] may still be added.
mantra: Choose, explore from index + 1, un-choose.
pitfalls: Save path.copy(); saving path itself stores one list that ends up empty.
visit(index + 1) uses each value once; visit(index) allows reuse; visit(start + 1) is the classic bug.
Duplicate values: sort first, then skip values[index] == values[index - 1] when index > start.

anchors.name: Subsets
anchors.trick: Exactly this.

anchors.name: Subsets II
anchors.trick: Sort; skip a repeated value when index > start.

anchors.name: Combination Sum
anchors.trick: Recurse with visit(index) to reuse a value; stop when the remainder goes negative.

anchors.name: Permutations
anchors.trick: No start index: loop over every value and skip those in a used set.

mutations.explanation: Saves the same list object every time; after backtracking, every saved subset is empty.
Recurses from the loop start instead of past the chosen index, so values repeat and subsets are duplicated.

title: Heap: top k largest
summary: The k largest values, largest first. Keep a min-heap of at most k values; its root is the smallest survivor, the bar a new value must beat. O(n log k).
triggers: k largest, smallest, most frequent or closest
a stream where only the best k matter
prompts: A game server receives scores all day. Keep the ten highest scores so far without storing every score.
From thousands of delivery stops, return the five closest to the depot.
invariant: heap holds the k largest values seen so far, and heap[0] is the smallest of them.
mantra: Keep k in a min-heap; the root is the bar to beat.
pitfalls: heapq is min-only: push -value, or (-key, tiebreak, item), for a max-heap.
Tuples compare field by field; add an index tiebreak when items can't be compared.
Once the heap is full, heapq.heappushpop(heap, value) pushes and pops in one step.
Only heap[0] is ordered; sort the heap to return it in order.

anchors.name: Kth Largest Element in an Array
anchors.trick: Size-k min-heap; heap[0] is the answer.

anchors.name: Top K Frequent Elements
anchors.trick: Counter first, then a size-k heap of (count, value).

anchors.name: K Closest Points to Origin
anchors.trick: Size-k max-heap keyed by -(x * x + y * y); skip the square root.

anchors.name: Merge k Sorted Lists
anchors.trick: Min-heap of (value, list index, node) frontiers.

mutations.explanation: Pops as soon as the heap reaches k, so only k - 1 values survive.

title: Union-find: path halving, union by size
summary: Merge groups of nodes 0..n-1 and ask whether two share a group. find() halves the path as it climbs; union() hangs the smaller root under the larger and returns False when already joined. Near O(1) amortized.
triggers: groups that only ever merge, with 'are x and y connected?' queries
adding undirected edges one at a time and spotting the first cycle
prompts: Accounts that share an email address belong to the same person. After all merges, how many distinct people remain?
Cables are added between servers one at a time. Report the first cable that closes a loop.
invariant: Following parent pointers from any node reaches its group's root, and size[root] is that group's size.
mantra: Find both roots; hang the smaller under the larger.
pitfalls: Union the roots, never the raw nodes.
This is path halving (parent = grandparent), not full path compression; both give near-constant time.
Count components as n minus the successful unions.
union() returning False means the edge closes a cycle.

anchors.name: Number of Provinces
anchors.trick: Union every connected pair; provinces = n - successful unions.

anchors.name: Redundant Connection
anchors.trick: The first edge whose union returns False.

anchors.name: Accounts Merge
anchors.trick: Union accounts that share an email, then group emails by root.

mutations.explanation: Uses parents instead of roots: two nodes deep in one tree look like different groups, and a subtree gets re-hung.

title: 1D DP: take or skip
summary: Largest sum of nonnegative values with no two adjacent. dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + values[i]), rolled into two variables. O(n) time, O(1) space.
code:
# Choose between skipping this value and taking it.
def max_nonadjacent_sum(values):
    previous_two = 0
    previous_one = 0
    for value in values:
        current = max(previous_one, previous_two + value)
        previous_two = previous_one
        previous_one = current
    return previous_one
triggers: maximize, minimize or count over choices where taking one blocks its neighbour
a recursion that recomputes the same prefix or suffix
prompts: A runner may train on any day but never two days in a row, and each day's session has a fitness score. Maximize the total score.
Billboard slots along a road each pay a fee, but neighbouring slots can't both be rented. Choose slots to maximize income.
invariant: After each value, previous_one is the best total for the prefix so far and previous_two the best for the prefix one shorter.
mantra: Take it plus two back, or skip it and keep one back.
pitfalls: Shift previous_two before overwriting previous_one, or use a tuple assignment.
Write the full recurrence and base case first, then roll the table into variables.
If at least one value must be taken, the empty-choice base of 0 is wrong for all-negative input.

anchors.name: House Robber
anchors.trick: Exactly this.

anchors.name: House Robber II
anchors.trick: Circular street: best of values[1:] and values[:-1].

anchors.name: Climbing Stairs
anchors.trick: Same two-variable roll with + instead of max.

anchors.name: Min Cost Climbing Stairs
anchors.trick: dp[i] = cost[i] + min(dp[i-1], dp[i-2]).

mutations.explanation: Adds value to a total that may already include its neighbour.
Both variables end up holding dp[i], so the next value is added next to its neighbour.

title: 0/1 knapsack: capacity loop backward
summary: Most value from (weight, value) items within a capacity, each item used at most once. One row of best totals by capacity; walk capacities downward so an item never builds on itself. O(n × capacity).
triggers: choose a subset of items under a weight, cost or size budget, each item at most once
can some subset reach exactly this sum?
prompts: A hiker's pack holds a fixed weight. Each piece of gear has a weight and a usefulness score, and there is only one of each. Pack the most useful load.
A studio has a fixed number of hours this week and a list of possible commissions, each with the hours it needs and a fee. Each can be taken at most once. Maximize the fees.
invariant: After an item is processed, best[c] is the most value that fits in capacity c using only the items seen so far, each at most once.
mantra: Each item once: walk capacity down.
pitfalls: Walking capacity upward reuses the item in the same pass; that is unbounded knapsack.
The loop stops at weight: smaller capacities can't hold the item.
best starts at 0 everywhere because taking nothing is always allowed.

anchors.name: Partition Equal Subset Sum
anchors.trick: Boolean version: can a subset reach sum // 2? Same backward loop.

anchors.name: Target Sum
anchors.trick: Count subsets that sum to (total + target) / 2 with the same backward loop.

anchors.name: Last Stone Weight II
anchors.trick: Find the reachable subset sum closest to half the total.

anchors.name: Ones and Zeroes
anchors.trick: Two capacities, zeros and ones, both walked backward.

mutations.explanation: Walking upward lets best[c - weight] already include this item, so one item can be taken many times.

title: Unbounded knapsack: fewest coins
summary: Fewest coins that make an amount, with unlimited coins of each value, or -1. dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a - coin] + 1), walking amounts upward so a coin can be reused. O(len(coins) × amount).
triggers: fewest pieces, or the number of ways, to build a total from reusable parts
an unlimited supply of each item and a target sum
prompts: A vending machine gives change in a few coin values and never runs out of any. What is the smallest number of coins that pays out an exact amount?
Floor tiles come in a handful of lengths, unlimited of each. Cover a corridor of exact length with as few tiles as possible, or report that it can't be done.
invariant: After a coin is processed, dp[a] is the fewest coins that make a using only the coins seen so far, repeats allowed.
mantra: Reuse allowed: walk the amount up, plus one coin.
pitfalls: Seed dp[0] = 0 and every other amount with infinity; amounts never reached stay infinite and become -1.
Walking amounts upward reuses a coin; walking downward allows each coin once (0/1 knapsack).
Counting ways adds instead of taking the minimum, with coins in the outer loop so each combination is counted once.

anchors.name: Coin Change
anchors.trick: Exactly this.

anchors.name: Coin Change II
anchors.trick: Count ways: dp[a] += dp[a - coin], coins in the outer loop.

anchors.name: Perfect Squares
anchors.trick: The coins are the squares up to n.

anchors.name: Combination Sum IV
anchors.trick: Amounts in the outer loop count ordered sequences instead.

mutations.explanation: Forgets to count the coin just used, so every reachable amount reports 0 coins.
Walking downward allows each coin at most once, so amounts that need a repeated coin look impossible.

title: Factory: a registry of creators
summary: create(kind) looks the class up in a registry that each class joins with @register, so a new channel never edits create(). An unknown kind raises instead of quietly falling back.
triggers: the caller knows a kind, name or config value, not the class to construct
an if/elif that picks a class by a type string and grows with every new type
prompts: A settings file lists export formats by name, such as csv or json. The app must construct the right exporter for each name, and adding a format must not touch the code that reads the settings.
A game level file names its enemies by type, such as goblin or archer. The loader must create the right object for each name, and other developers will add enemy types without editing the loader.
invariant: create() reads only the registry: every kind it can build was registered by its class, and any other kind raises.
mantra: Look the class up; don't branch on the name.
pitfalls: A class decorator must return the class, or the module-level name becomes None.
Return CHANNELS[kind](), a new instance, not the class itself.
Raise on an unknown kind; a silent default turns typos into wrong behaviour.

anchors.name: Notification service
anchors.trick: Each channel name maps to a sender class that registers itself.

anchors.name: Parking lot
anchors.trick: One factory call turns a vehicle type into the matching spot or ticket.

mutations.explanation: Returns the class instead of a new instance, so callers get no object to send with.
Falls back to email for an unknown kind, hiding typos that should fail loudly.

title: Builder: assemble, then validate once
summary: Each step returns the builder, so optional parts chain in any order. build() rejects a query with no columns and hands back an immutable snapshot that later steps can't change.
triggers: an object with many optional parts, set in any order, that must be valid once finished
a constructor with a long list of mostly optional parameters
prompts: A report screen lets users pick columns, add any number of filters and optionally cap the row count, in whatever order they click. A report with no columns chosen must be refused before it runs.
A game lets players set up a character across several screens: name, class, starting items. Nothing should exist until the final screen confirms the choices are valid.
invariant: Every step returns the builder; only build() creates a query, after one validation, and the query never shares a list with the builder.
mantra: Set in any order, check once, hand back a copy.
pitfalls: Each step must return self, or the chain breaks at the next call.
Copy lists into the product with tuple(); a shared list lets later steps change a finished query.
Don't name a method after a field: with self.limit as data, a limit() method would be hidden.

anchors.name: Pizza or burger ordering
anchors.trick: Add toppings step by step; build() validates and prices the order.

anchors.name: HTTP client request
anchors.trick: Headers, body and timeout chained before one build().

mutations.explanation: Hands out the builder's own list, so selecting another column later changes a query that was already built.
An empty list is not None, so the check never fires and a query with no columns gets built.

title: Singleton: one shared instance
summary: Config() always returns the same object. Check, take the class lock, check again, then build once. Settings are created in __new__ because __init__ would run again on every call.
triggers: exactly one shared object for the whole process, such as a config, registry or connection pool
'only one may ever exist', even when several threads ask for it at the same moment
prompts: Every part of an app reads feature switches from one in-memory table loaded on first use. Separate tables would disagree, so every module must receive the very same table.
A print spooler must keep exactly one job queue, no matter how many worker threads ask for it first.
invariant: At most one instance is ever created, under the class lock, and every call returns that same object.
mantra: Check, lock, check again, then build once.
pitfalls: Share one class-level lock; a lock made inside __new__ is new on every call and guards nothing.
Without the second check, a thread that waited for the lock builds another instance.
Python runs __init__ after every Config() call; set state up once in __new__, or later calls wipe it.

anchors.name: Logger
anchors.trick: One shared logger whose handlers are configured once.

anchors.name: Parking lot
anchors.trick: One ParkingLot object owns every floor and spot.

mutations.explanation: A lock created on each call is never shared, so two threads can still build two instances.

title: Adapter: translate an interface you can't change
summary: The checkout calls pay(dollars); the vendor's SDK wants cents and reports declines in a dict. The adapter converts units and raises on a decline. The vendor class is given; you type the adapter.
triggers: existing code expects one interface, and a library or legacy class offers a different one you can't edit
translating units, names or result shapes at a boundary, such as cents and dollars or status codes and exceptions
prompts: Your app logs through log(level, message), but the monitoring vendor's client only offers emit(severity_code, payload). Make the app's calls reach the vendor without changing either side.
A new thermometer driver reports Fahrenheit through read_f(), while every dashboard calls celsius(). Plug the new device in without touching the dashboards.
invariant: Callers see only pay(dollars); every unit, name and failure translation happens inside the adapter, and the vendor class is never edited.
mantra: Wrap it, translate it, never edit it.
pitfalls: Convert units with round(dollars * 100); int() truncates 0.29 * 100 to 28.
Translate failures too: raise your own error instead of leaking the vendor's status dict.
Hold the vendor object rather than subclassing it, so its whole API doesn't leak into yours.

anchors.name: Payment gateway integration
anchors.trick: One adapter per provider behind a single pay() interface.

anchors.name: Third-party logging or maps SDK
anchors.trick: Adapt the vendor's calls so the rest of the code never imports the SDK.

mutations.explanation: Passes dollars where the vendor expects cents, so a $12.34 payment charges 12.34 cents.
A non-empty dict is always truthy, so declined charges come back as successes.

title: Decorator: wrap to add behaviour
summary: Cheese and HappyHour wrap anything with cost() and describe() and offer the same two methods, so they stack in any order. Each calls through, then adds its part. The base pizza is given.
triggers: add optional features to an object at runtime, in any combination, without a subclass per combination
wrappers that keep the same interface: logging, caching, retries, add-ons
prompts: An HTTP client needs optional retries, request logging and auth headers. Teams combine them differently, and nobody wants a class for every combination.
A document exporter can add a header, a footer and page numbers in any combination the user ticks, and new options keep arriving.
invariant: Every wrapper offers the wrapped object's methods and calls through to it, adding its own part before or after.
mantra: Same interface in and out: call through, then add.
pitfalls: A wrapper that never calls the wrapped object replaces it instead of decorating it.
Order matters: HappyHour(Cheese(pizza)) discounts the cheese too; Cheese(HappyHour(pizza)) doesn't.
A subclass per combination (CheesePizza, CheeseHappyHourPizza, ...) explodes; wrap objects instead.

anchors.name: Coffee or pizza ordering
anchors.trick: Each add-on wraps the item and adds its price and name.

anchors.name: Notification service
anchors.trick: Wrap a base notifier with SMS and Slack senders in any combination.

mutations.explanation: Returns only its own price; a decorator must call through to the wrapped item and add to its result.
Hard-codes the base instead of asking the wrapped item, so every topping underneath vanishes from the description.

title: Composite: one interface for parts and wholes
summary: A File and a Folder both answer size(). A folder sums whatever its children answer, so nesting works at any depth and callers never check which one they hold.
triggers: a tree of parts and wholes where callers want one operation on a single item or a whole group
recursive structures: folders and files, menus and submenus, org charts, nested expressions
prompts: A drawing app lets users group shapes, and groups can hold other groups. Moving or measuring a group must work exactly like moving or measuring a single shape.
An org chart rolls up salary cost: a manager's cost includes everyone below them at any depth, while an individual's cost is just their own salary.
invariant: File and Folder answer the same size(); a folder's answer is the sum of its children's answers, at any depth.
mantra: Leaves answer; groups ask their children.
pitfalls: isinstance checks in the folder or the caller defeat the pattern; give leaf and group the same method.
Call child.size(), not child.bytes, or nested folders count as nothing.
Don't store an attribute named like a method: self.size = size would hide size().

anchors.name: File system
anchors.trick: Folder.size() sums its children; File.size() returns its bytes.

anchors.name: Restaurant menu
anchors.trick: Menus hold items and submenus; print or price the whole tree with one call.

mutations.replacement: return sum(child.bytes for child in self.children if isinstance(child, File))
mutations.explanation: Counts only the files directly inside; nested folders add nothing because the folder stopped asking its children.
Returns the child, so a chained add() puts the next item inside it, or fails on a file.

title: Strategy: swap the rule, keep the caller
summary: Checkout holds a pricing object and calls its apply(); the caller picks the rule and can swap it at runtime. A new discount is a new class, never a new branch in Checkout.
triggers: several interchangeable ways to do one job, chosen by the caller or by config at runtime
an if/elif on a mode or type value inside one method that keeps growing
prompts: A maps app offers fastest, shortest and no-toll routes. The navigation screen asks for a route without knowing which rule the user picked, and a scenic option is coming next month.
A warehouse picks orders by arrival, by priority or by shelf location, and managers switch the rule during the day without restarting anything.
invariant: Checkout knows only the apply() interface; the caller chooses the rule, and adding a rule never edits Checkout.
mantra: Pass the rule in; never branch on it.
pitfalls: The context must call the strategy it holds; a hard-coded rule makes swapping pointless.
Strategies don't pick their successor; when the object switches itself, that's State.
In Python a plain function can be the strategy; a class helps when the rule has settings, like a percent.

anchors.name: Parking lot
anchors.trick: A fee strategy per vehicle type or time of day, passed into the ticket.

anchors.name: Splitwise
anchors.trick: Equal, exact and percentage splits as interchangeable split strategies.

mutations.explanation: Checkout ignores the rule it was given and hard-codes one, so swapping strategies changes nothing.
Charges the discount instead of what's left: 25% off becomes paying 25%.

title: State: let the current state answer
summary: A vending machine hands each event to its current state object. Idle accepts a coin and switches to Paid; Paid dispenses and switches back. The machine never checks a status flag.
triggers: the same call behaves differently depending on the object's current mode, with rules for which mode comes next
status flags checked by if/elif in every method: vending machines, order lifecycles, traffic lights
prompts: A turnstile ignores pushes until a ticket is scanned, lets exactly one person through, then locks again. Extra scans while it's unlocked must not bank extra passes.
A document moves from draft to review to published. Editing is allowed only in draft, approving only in review, and each step decides where the document goes next.
invariant: The machine always holds exactly one state object; each event is answered by that state, and only states change machine.state.
mantra: Ask the state; the state picks the next state.
pitfalls: Assign machine.state, not self.state: the state is handed the machine so it can switch it.
Every state answers every event, even if only to refuse it.
If the caller picks the object and it never replaces itself, that's Strategy.

anchors.name: Vending machine
anchors.trick: Idle, paid and sold-out states each handle coin and button events.

anchors.name: Elevator system
anchors.trick: Idle, moving and doors-open states decide what each button press does.

mutations.explanation: Sets an attribute on the state object instead of the machine, so the machine never leaves Idle.
Stays paid after dispensing, so every later press dispenses for free.

title: Observer: notify every subscriber
summary: Subscribers hand the feed a callback and get back a function that unsubscribes them. publish() loops over a copy of the list, so a callback can unsubscribe mid-publish without skipping its neighbour.
triggers: one change must reach many dependents, and the source shouldn't know who they are
subscribe and unsubscribe, listeners, event handlers: 'notify everyone when X changes'
prompts: When a flight's gate changes, the departure board, the mobile app and the crew pager all need the new gate. Next quarter a chat bot will want it too, and the gate system must not change.
A spreadsheet cell feeds several charts. Whenever the value changes every chart showing it redraws, and closing a chart stops its updates.
invariant: publish calls each callback that was subscribed when it started, exactly once, and the feed never depends on what a callback does.
mantra: Keep a list; notify a copy.
pitfalls: Loop over a copy: a callback that unsubscribes during publish would make the live loop skip its neighbour.
Unsubscribe removes this callback; forgotten subscriptions keep their objects alive.
A slow or failing callback holds up the rest; real systems queue or isolate them.

anchors.name: Stock price alerts
anchors.trick: Traders subscribe to a ticker; each price update notifies them.

anchors.name: Notification service
anchors.trick: Order events fan out to email, SMS and analytics subscribers.

mutations.explanation: Loops over the live list: a subscriber that unsubscribes during publish makes the loop skip the next one.
Unsubscribing removes whoever subscribed last, not this callback.

title: Command: actions you can undo
summary: Each edit is an object with do() and undo(). The editor keeps two stacks: undo moves the last command from done to undone, redo moves it back, and a new command clears redo.
triggers: undo and redo, macros, or a log of user actions that must be stored and replayed
separate what triggers an action (a button, shortcut or menu) from the code that performs it
prompts: A drawing app lets users move, recolour and delete shapes, then step backwards and forwards through those changes as far as they like.
A smart-home hub records the actions a scene performs, so one tap can roll the whole scene back in reverse order.
invariant: done holds applied commands in order and undone holds undone ones; undo and redo move one command between them, and a new command empties undone.
mantra: Every action knows its inverse; a new action clears redo.
pitfalls: A new command must clear the redo stack; redoing old commands onto newer text corrupts it.
undo must reverse exactly what do changed: the whole inserted text, at its position.
Undo in reverse order by popping from the end of the history.

anchors.name: Text editor with undo and redo
anchors.trick: Insert and delete commands on two stacks.

anchors.name: Remote control or smart home
anchors.trick: Buttons hold commands; the last command can be undone.

mutations.explanation: Clears the undo history instead of the redo stack, so nothing before this edit can be undone.
Undo removes one character instead of the whole inserted text.

title: Chain of responsibility: handle it or pass it on
summary: Approvers are linked by spending limit. Each approves what it can and forwards the rest unchanged; the caller knows only the first link, and the end of the chain rejects.
triggers: the first of several handlers able to deal with a request should take it, tried in order, without the sender choosing
escalation levels, middleware and fallbacks: approvals by amount, support tiers, cash dispensers
prompts: Support tickets go to a chatbot first; whatever it can't answer goes to a first-line agent, then to an engineer. Customers only submit the ticket and never pick the level.
A loan request is reviewed by an automatic scorer, then a branch officer, then a credit committee, and the first one allowed to decide on that amount does.
invariant: Each approver either answers or forwards the unchanged request to its successor; exactly one link answers, or the end of the chain rejects.
mantra: Handle it or hand it on.
pitfalls: Forward by calling the successor's approve(), so the request keeps travelling.
Decide what the end of the chain does: reject, return a default or raise.
Unlike a decorator, a handler that answers stops the chain; unlike an observer, only one handler acts.

anchors.name: Expense approval workflow
anchors.trick: Manager, director and CFO links, each with a spending limit.

mutations.explanation: Names the next approver without asking it, so every amount above the manager's limit lands on the director, even 1,000,000.
Off by one at the limit: a manager may approve exactly 1,000, but this escalates it.

title: LRU cache: evict the least recently used
summary: An OrderedDict keeps keys from least to most recently used. get and put move the key to the end; when the cache overflows, popitem(last=False) evicts from the front. O(1) per operation.
triggers: a fixed-size cache that evicts whatever was used longest ago
O(1) get and put that also track recency: a hash map plus an ordered list
prompts: A photo app keeps thumbnails for the 200 images viewed most recently. Opening an old image again must protect it from being the next one dropped.
A database client caches query results but has room for a few hundred. When it's full, it discards the result nobody has asked for in the longest time.
invariant: items holds at most capacity keys ordered from least to most recently used, and every get or put moves its key to the end.
mantra: Touch moves to the back; evict from the front.
pitfalls: popitem() takes the newest entry by default; LRU eviction needs popitem(last=False).
Assigning to an existing key keeps its old position, so move it to the end after updating.
Without OrderedDict, use a dict of nodes and a doubly linked list with head and tail sentinels.

anchors.name: LRU Cache
anchors.trick: Exactly this; interviewers may ask for the linked-list version.

anchors.name: LFU Cache
anchors.trick: Group keys by use count, with LRU order inside each count.

mutations.explanation: popitem() takes from the end by default, evicting the key that was just put instead of the least recently used one.
Moving a read key to the front marks it least recent, so the key you just used is evicted next.

title: Rate limiter: token bucket
summary: Tokens refill with elapsed time, capped at capacity; a request spends one whole token or is refused. The clock is passed in so tests control time. O(1) per request.
code:
# Refill by elapsed time up to capacity; a request spends one token or is refused.
class TokenBucket:
    def __init__(self, capacity, per_second, clock):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.per_second = per_second
        self.clock = clock
        self.tokens = capacity
        self.updated = clock()

    def allow(self):
        now = self.clock()
        self.tokens = min(self.capacity, self.tokens + (now - self.updated) * self.per_second)
        self.updated = now
        if self.tokens < 1:
            return False
        self.tokens -= 1
        return True
triggers: allow at most N requests per period with short bursts, per user or per API key
throttling, quotas and 'too many requests' errors
prompts: A public API lets each key make a burst of ten calls, then roughly one call per second. Calls beyond the allowance get an error instead of waiting.
A game server lets each player fire a few shots in quick succession but limits sustained firing, so scripted clicking gains nothing.
invariant: Before each decision tokens = min(capacity, tokens + elapsed × rate); a request is allowed only when a whole token is available, and it spends that token.
mantra: Refill by elapsed time, cap it, spend one.
pitfalls: Cap the refill at capacity, or an idle client banks an unlimited burst.
Record the refill time on every call, or the same seconds are credited twice.
Inject the clock so tests control time, and keep one bucket per user or key.

anchors.name: API rate limiter
anchors.trick: One bucket per key: burst = capacity, sustained rate = refill.

anchors.name: Logger Rate Limiter
anchors.trick: A simpler rule: remember when each message may print again.

anchors.name: Design Hit Counter
anchors.trick: A sliding window of timestamps instead of tokens.

mutations.explanation: Without the cap, a long idle period banks unlimited tokens and allows a burst far beyond capacity.
Allows a request with only part of a token, so the bucket runs into debt and lets traffic through too early.

title: Find and search files
summary: Find files by pattern and modification time, with recursive grep across codebases.
code:
# Find files by pattern and modification time
find . -type f -name "*.log" -mtime +7

# Search recursively for a string with line numbers
grep -rni --exclude-dir=node_modules "connection refused" ./src

# Find and count files matching an extension
find ./data -type f -name "*.json" | wc -l

title: Archives and remote transfers
summary: Compress and unpack tarballs, synchronize directories with rsync, and test HTTP endpoints.
code:

# Extract an archive to a destination folder

# Synchronize files while preserving permissions and showing progress

    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"status":"deployed"}'

    begin

title: String formatting and regex scanning
summary: Interpolate strings, match patterns with regular expressions, and extract capture groups.
code:
def parse_log_line(line)
    pattern = /^\[(\w+)\]\s+(\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2})\s+-\s+(.+)$/
    match = line.match(pattern)
    return nil unless match

    level, date, message = match.captures
    { level: level.downcase.to_sym, date: date, message: message }
end

title: Thread pool and futures
summary: Submit independent tasks and retrieve results in input order. Threads commonly suit blocking I/O; this arithmetic task only demonstrates the API.
code:
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

def square(value):
    return value * value

def parallel_squares(values):
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as executor:
        futures = [executor.submit(square, value) for value in values]
        return [future.result() for future in futures]

title: Async tasks with gather
summary: Await cooperative work without blocking the event loop. gather returns results in argument order. Run the demo from a normal Python script.
code:
import asyncio

async def work(value):
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    return value * 2

async def run_batch(values):
    tasks = [work(value) for value in values]
    return await asyncio.gather(*tasks)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(asyncio.run(run_batch([1, 2, 3])))
